## One in sixteen

A 64-byte line holds `64 / 4 = 16` ints. Walking the array one element at a time, the access to `a[0]` misses and the whole line containing `a[0]` through `a[15]` is fetched. The next fifteen accesses hit in that line. Then `a[16]` misses, and the pattern repeats.

So one access in sixteen misses:

```
miss rate = 1 / (line size / element size)
          = 1 / (64 / 4)
          = 1 / 16
          = 0.0625 = 6.25%
```

### Why this is the most useful number in the subject

Notice what the miss rate depends on: **the element size and the line size**, and nothing else. Not the array length, not the cache capacity. A sequential walk over data that does not fit in cache has a miss rate fixed by the geometry of the line.

That gives you a reference point to compare any real measurement against. If you measure a sequential loop and see a miss rate near 6.25% on 4-byte elements, the loop is doing as well as a sequential walk can. If you see something close to 100%, you are not really walking sequentially — the stride is bigger than you think, or you are chasing pointers, or the array-of-structs layout means each "element" is far apart in memory.

### The two obvious variations

- **`double` instead of `int`** — 8-byte elements, so `64 / 8 = 8` per line, and the miss rate doubles to `1/8`. Bigger elements means fewer per line means more misses per element touched.
- **A stride of 16 ints instead of 1** — now every access lands on a fresh line, and the miss rate is **100%**, fetching 64 bytes to use 4 of them. This is the same loop doing sixteen times the memory traffic for the same arithmetic, and it is the single most common reason a loop is slower than it looks.

Real hardware does better than the first case, because the prefetcher recognises a sequential stream and fetches lines before you ask. That is why the problem rules prefetching out: it changes the measured answer, but not the geometry the answer comes from.
